title: Calcutta High Court: suit on settlement of decretal dues from a sale of goods is a commercial dispute under the 2015 Act
meta_description: Calcutta HC, 29 Sept 2026: a suit on a settlement of decretal dues from a sale of goods is a commercial dispute under the 2015 Act.
case_name: M. Walter and Co. and Others v. Rajashi Developers Private Limited
body: The Calcutta High Court has held that a suit to recover money promised under a settlement agreement, where that money stands for dues under a decree, can be a commercial dispute under Section 2(1)(c)(xviii) of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015. Justice Ananya Bandyopadhyay decided M. Walter and Co. and Others v. Rajashi Developers Private Limited on 29 September 2026. The Court directed the Registrar, Original Side, to convert the suit into a commercial suit and give it a definite number within a fortnight. The matter was fixed for hearing on 17 November 2026.

Behind the suit lies a decree that arose from an earlier dispute over a sale of goods. While execution of that decree was pending, the parties signed a settlement agreement dated 1 November 2022. Rajashi Developers undertook to pay Rs 55,00,000 towards full and final settlement of the decretal dues, and withdrawal of the execution proceeding was the other side of the bargain. When the payment was not made, the claimants sued on the settlement agreement for recovery. The suit sits on the Original Side of the Calcutta High Court, which is where the question of classification arose.

Classification was the only point for decision, and it was narrow. Clause (xviii) of Section 2(1)(c) brings agreements connected with the sale of goods within the definition of a commercial dispute. A settlement agreement does not itself sell anything. It records a promise to pay money that is owed because of an earlier transaction, and it ends a pending proceeding. The reported framing of the issue was whether such an agreement, taken alone, is the source of the claim, or whether the claim should be traced to the dealing that the agreement was made to settle.

Justice Bandyopadhyay chose the second approach. It looked past the settlement agreement and traced the commercial character of the claim to the transaction that the agreement expressly sought to settle. It also gave weight to the way the arrangement came about: the defendant entered it during execution and undertook payment of the decretal dues in return for the withdrawal of that execution. On that footing, the Court held that the suit is a commercial dispute within Section 2(1)(c)(xviii).

A stated limit qualifies the holding. It is made subject to the other statutory requirements that govern a commercial suit, and the reports reviewed do not list which of those requirements were examined or met. The headnote on one of the reporting sites records that the judgment refers to Section 2(1)(c) with its Explanation, Section 12A of the Act, Section 62 of the Indian Contract Act and Order VII Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Those references indicate the arguments that were available to both sides. The reports do not say how each provision was applied, and the full text should be read before anyone relies on a particular step of the reasoning.

For practitioners in Kolkata, the practical effect is on the track the suit follows. A suit classified as commercial is dealt with under the special procedure of the 2015 Act, with its stricter handling of pleadings and its provision for pre-institution mediation, instead of the ordinary civil procedure. A settlement agreement that compromises a decree is a common way for a money dispute to continue after judgment. The decision supports the view that the commercial label can survive such a compromise when the debt behind it came from a commercial transaction, and that a party should not assume the label is lost merely because the plaint is drafted on the settlement.

Two cautions apply. First, this is a decision of a single judge on the Original Side, and it turns on the particular settlement, which expressly referred to the decree and to the withdrawal of execution. A settlement that recites no such link may be argued differently. Second, the Court's own wording keeps the other statutory conditions open, so a plaint that fits clause (xviii) must still satisfy the rest of the Act. No report reviewed mentions an appeal or a stay, but the full judgment has not been read for this note and its status should be checked on the court's records before it is cited.
why_it_matters: The ruling shows how a Kolkata Original Side judge treats a suit founded on a compromise of a decree. The commercial character was traced to the original sale of goods and not to the settlement document alone. That affects the forum, the procedure and the pre-institution steps for money claims that follow a settled execution. It is a single-judge view, tied to the facts of one settlement, and the other statutory conditions for a commercial suit remain open.
card_summary: Calcutta High Court holds that a suit on a settlement agreement for decretal dues from a sale of goods is a commercial dispute under Section 2(1)(c)(xviii); the suit was converted into a commercial suit.
card_tip: Check whether the settlement recites the original goods transaction and the withdrawal of execution, since the Court relied on that link.
